clue.text: Don's shaking, etc, being ensnared by siren

indicators.note: to be ensnared is to be caught inside a trap, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a siren lures sailors to their doom

indicators.note: something shaking is jolted about, so its letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A university fellow trembles, lured in by some seductive woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is': the don is what the wordplay makes. ETC is shuffled to ECT and placed after the first letter of LURER.
explanation.definitionFit: At Oxford and Cambridge a don is a college teacher, someone who gives talks to students.

clue.text: One is, in a different form, unknown mountain-dweller

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
be is the infinitive form of the verb whose third person is 'is'
x is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A cryptic remark about some unknown creature of the peaks that keeps changing shape.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibex is a wild goat with long curved horns living among crags in the Alps and other ranges.

clue.text: Experience drug overdose, getting support

parts.note: a trip is the hallucinatory experience of taking a drug like LSD
the standard abbreviation for an overdose

explanation.surface: Someone takes too much of a drug and ends up needing help.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-legged stand holds a camera or telescope steady, so it is a kind of brace.

clue.text: Carriage direction

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the way a person holds and carries themselves, their posture
second meaning: a compass heading taken in navigation

explanation.walkthrough: Carriage suggests a railway coach, but here it means deportment.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a person's deportment or posture and a navigator's compass heading.

clue.text: Part of the whole embarrassment of 'relating'

indicators.note: an embarrassment is a state of confusion, so the quoted word is thrown into disorder

parts.note: the quoted word supplies the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Telling a story can be awkward, it seems, when all of it comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something integral is essential to and forms a necessary component of a complete entity.

clue.text: Criminal in court — man's not at all like Keats!

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked or bent out of shape, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A villain in the dock is the opposite of a dreamy poet.
explanation.walkthrough: John Keats was one of the great English Romantic poets, so being unlike him means lacking romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats epitomises the Romantic movement and lovesick verse, so his opposite is prosaic and lacking in sentiment.

clue.text: Male milk producer is over a lot

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for male

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a dairy produces milk

explanation.surface: A man running a dairy has plenty on his plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A myriad is a countless or very great number of things, a huge quantity.

clue.text: No beer, as Dicky is on the drink

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the letters are in poor order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Somebody named Dicky is drinking but has no beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is a colloquial name for the sea, not alcohol. Dicky is British slang for shaky or unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: The drink is jocular slang for the sea, so travelling over it means being carried by ocean waves.

clue.text: North American news, plus tip from family nurse

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for north
A is a standard abbreviation for American
N is an abbreviation for new, as in news
'n' stands for and, as in rock 'n' roll

indicators.note: a tip is an extreme end, here the final point of the word that follows

parts.note: the final letter of family

explanation.surface: An American newspaper story about the person who looks after a household's children.
explanation.walkthrough: The tip of a word could be either end; here it is the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanny is a woman employed to care for children in their own home, a children's nurse.

clue.text: Jams broadcast giving access to the underworld

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard rather than read, so it is the sound that counts

parts.note: to jam is to become stuck fast

explanation.surface: Some radio signal is jammed, and it seems to open a door to the criminal world.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the dead were ferried across this river by Charon to reach Hades.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology the river Styx forms the boundary that souls cross to enter Hades.

clue.text: Old capital, per se? Polish virtually

indicators.note: virtually means almost, so the word is not quite complete and loses its end

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before it is trimmed; that the result runs straight through these clue words is a coincidence of the charade, not a hiding device

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about an ancient city and whether it is, in itself, nearly Polish.
explanation.walkthrough: Polish looks like the nationality, but it is just the word to be shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: Persepolis was the ceremonial seat of the ancient Achaemenid Persian empire, now ruins in Iran.

clue.text: Fellow at stern is very cold

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
stern and rigid both mean strict and unbending

explanation.surface: A man standing at the back of a ship feels the chill.
explanation.walkthrough: Stern looks like the back of a boat, but it is the adjective meaning strict.
explanation.definitionFit: Frigid describes intensely low temperatures, as in a freezing Arctic climate.

clue.text: Biscuit from Sandy's pile

parts.note: sandy hair is ginger, so Sandy is a nickname like Ginger
the nap is the raised pile on cloth such as velvet

explanation.surface: Someone called Sandy has a heap of cookies.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy looks like a person's name; it stands for the reddish hair colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A gingersnap is a crisp, spiced cookie flavoured with powdered root of the zingiber plant.

clue.text: Negative Frenchman in hot region abroad

parts.note: no is the negative answer

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: hot in the sense of sexually eager; randy is British for lustful
M is the abbreviation for monsieur

explanation.surface: A grumpy Frenchman finds himself in some sweltering foreign area.
explanation.walkthrough: Frenchman tempts you to write NORMAN, but it is just M, sitting inside the second letter group after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Normandy is a historic province of northern France, foreign territory from a British setter's viewpoint.

clue.text: Name involved in racial slur, like 'brainbox'

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it
slurred speech runs sounds together badly, so the letters come out muddled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Someone is named in connection with an offensive insult aimed at a clever person.
explanation.walkthrough: Brainbox is informal for the skull as well as for a clever person; the quotation marks flag the literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Cranial means relating to the skull, the bony case enclosing the brain.

clue.text: In a way, Brummie is attached to your old gemstone

parts.note: taken as written
Brummie is this puzzle's setter, so the setter refers to himself
thy is the archaic form of your
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Somehow a person from Birmingham is linked with your ancient jewel.
explanation.walkthrough: A Brummie is someone from Birmingham, but here it is the setter's pseudonym, giving ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Amethyst is a purple variety of quartz cut and polished for jewellery, a semi-precious stone.

clue.text: Spotted cloth by rocks

indicators.note: something that rocks is shaken back and forth, so the letters are disturbed

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Some fabric was noticed lying beside stones on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: Spotted looks like a verb meaning seen, but it is the adjective meaning marked with patches.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotchy skin or fabric is covered with irregular patches or marks of colour.

clue.text: Husband with bear grip

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
and means together with
to bear a weight is to hold it

explanation.surface: A married man wrestles with a grizzly.
explanation.definitionFit: A handhold is something to grasp for support, such as a ledge on a climbing wall.

clue.text: One large cut is limiting ex-queen's capital

indicators.note: to limit is to set bounds on all sides, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a means one
large cut down to its short form lg
taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the late Queen Elizabeth II

explanation.surface: A big budget cut restricts a former monarch's wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s in ex-queen's is part of the surface; the second word wraps around the late monarch's cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: Algiers is the chief city and seat of government of Algeria in North Africa.

clue.text: Neglectfully late wrapping present? Fine

indicators.note: wrapping goes around something, so one piece encloses the other
done neglectfully means done carelessly, so the letters are left in a mess

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
to be present is to be here

explanation.surface: Someone tardy with a gift-wrapped parcel is told that's all right.
explanation.walkthrough: Present suggests a gift to be wrapped, but it means being in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine here means delicate or airy, and ethereal describes something extremely light and insubstantial.

clue.text: Number of times to see the heartless grasping filthy rich

indicators.note: grasping holds something tight inside, so one piece encloses the other
without a heart means the central letter is taken out

parts.note: taken as written, before losing its middle letter

indicators.note: filthy suggests something messed up, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: How often must we watch the callous, greedy super-wealthy?
explanation.walkthrough: Filthy rich reads as one phrase, but filthy is the signal to rearrange rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrice means three times, a specific count of occasions, so it answers how many times.

clue.text: Line intersecting Sussex and Kent, etc. lacks power

parts.note: Sussex and Kent are counties in the South East of England
can't means is unable, lacks the power to

explanation.surface: A boundary across two English counties and others is ineffective.
explanation.walkthrough: Sussex and Kent are English counties south and east of London, so they stand for the SE region.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a secant is a straight line that cuts a curve at two or more points.

clue.text: Finch wrong to restrain runner

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold in check, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: a sin is a wrong
a ski is a runner on snow, like a sledge runner

explanation.surface: Somebody named Finch is wrong to hold back an athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: Runner suggests an athlete, but here it is a ski.
explanation.definitionFit: The siskin is a small yellowish-green songbird of the finch family.

clue.text: Put out hot vents that are concentrated on prey?

parts.note: being put out is being annoyed
H for hot, as on a tap
to vent an opinion is to air it

explanation.surface: An angry hunter blows off steam while stalking an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Put out and vents read like a fire and its smoke, but they mean annoyed and voices.
explanation.definitionFit: Crosshairs are the fine lines in a gun sight that a hunter centres on the target animal.

clue.text: Wind in roof — oh no!

indicators.note: in says the letters are found inside the words that follow

parts.note: the end of roof runs into oh and the start of no

explanation.surface: A gale gets under the roof, to someone's dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: The foehn is a warm dry wind blowing down the lee side of the Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: The fohn is a warm, dry downslope breeze in Alpine valleys, a named meteorological current of air.

clue.text: Relief (affordable) housing fuss

indicators.note: housing means holding inside, so the letters are sheltered within the words before it

parts.note: the end of relief joins the start of affordable

explanation.surface: There is a commotion about cheap homes being provided as relief.
explanation.walkthrough: Housing looks like part of the affordable housing scene, but it is the signal to look inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Faff is British informal for dithering or making a needless song and dance about something.

clue.text: Unrefined group needs to change its direction

indicators.note: a direction letter swaps for its opposite, left turning into right

parts.note: a class is a group, as of pupils

explanation.surface: A rough crowd must turn around and go the other way.
explanation.walkthrough: L for left becomes R for right in the word for group.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass means grossly lacking in sensitivity or taste, coarse and boorish.

clue.text: Rule soundly applied to trip that puts a damper on things

definitions.text: that puts a damper on things
definitions.note: a relative clause describing the noun answer

indicators.note: soundly here means by sound, so the spoken form counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: to reign is to rule as monarch
a trip is a stumble, a fall

explanation.surface: A rule is enforced on an outing, and it spoils the fun.
explanation.walkthrough: Puts a damper on reads as spoiling fun, but here it means literally making things wet.
explanation.definitionFit: Precipitation literally makes everything wet and damp, and a wet day also spoils outdoor events.
